arbol_de_trazas.nota: El árbol lo arman el `EjecutorDeEtapas` (corrida y etapa) y el decorador de puertos (una traza por llamada a puerto). **Ninguna etapa emite su propio span** — la observabilidad lo prohíbe y señala al ejecutor como el lugar correcto para el desglose. `campos_censurados > 0` es el registro de decisiones actuando: en una consulta ad-hoc no viaja ni el pedido ni la imagen.

politica.por_que: Las 30 consultas de evaluación se trazan **completas** (el registro de decisiones). No son dato de un tercero: son obras de nuestro propio held-out, versionadas con el ground truth porque son el **instrumento de medición** (el registro de decisiones). Trazarlas enteras cumple las técnicas avanzadas aisladas por medición, la tabla de tokens, costo y la figura y el criterio de costo sin tocar el compromiso de privacidad.

entrada.nota_de_retencion: el registro de decisiones (cierra la pregunta por el ciclo de vida de la corrida purgada): **no se persiste nada de un tercero**. Los bytes de la imagen no se guardan nunca —no hay clave que los active— y el `pedido` solo si `[retencion] pedido = true`. Lo que se vacía son **campos**, y que estaban vaciados queda registrado (la regla de qué se versiona): la corrida conserva su `corrida_id`, su ordinal, sus rankings y sus degradaciones, porque borrarla reasignaría el ordinal y un informe que cita la corrida #1 apuntaría a otra ejecución.

aic:43211.texto: Having been stripped of their images and whitewashed by Protestant reformers in the 16th century, the Dutch Republic’s large Gothic churches offered a compelling subject for artists. Emanuel de Witte was one of a small group of painters who specialized in explorations of the light, shade, and volume particular to church interiors. In this painting, executed late in the artist’s career, the organ and genealogical panels honoring the dead (suspended from the ceiling and affixed to the columns) are the only decoration.

aic:57049.texto: This painting is one of four depictions of architectural fantasies by Hubert Robert commissioned by the Marquis de Laborde for his elegant country estate at Méréville, south of Paris. It features a grandiose vaulted space that frames an obelisk, with a peristyle, or colonnade, closing off the distance. Through years of study in Italy, Robert absorbed the vocabulary of Classical architecture and sculpture into his own imaginative language. Here, the female ﬁgure in the central niche is based on a ﬁrst-century sculpture that the artist would have seen during his stay in Rome.

aic:57051.texto: The painting of Classical ruins had reached the zenith of its popularity when Hubert Robert, the leading French practitioner of this specialty, was commissioned in 1787 to paint a suite of four canvases for a wealthy financier’s château at Méréville, near Paris. The Fountains and its companion pieces were set into the paneled walls of a salon in the château, creating an alternate space that played off of the elegant, Neoclassical decor of the room. Robert has studied in Rome from 1754 to 1765 and there had gleaned his artistic vocabulary. Like the other three large paintings from the group painted for Méréville, all in the Art Institute, The Fountains exploits Robert’s typical vocabulary of fictive niches, arches, coffered vaults, colonnades, majestic stairwells, and Roman statuary to create a fantasy of expansive space. The four paintings are inhabited by tiny figures in the foreground; these serve only to set the scale and animate the scene, for the ruins themselves are the true subject of the pictures. In his use of ruins, Robert embodied the notion of the relationship of mankind and the built environment to nature that was expressed by the French philosopher and encyclopedist Denis Diderot: “Everything vanishes, everything dies, only time endures.”

cma:111691.texto: The Jewish synagogue was among Magnasco's most frequently painted subjects, here presented in a mystical and imaginative way. Expansive architectural space creates room for a multitude of tiny, fantastical figures with elongated limbs. These characters respond to the service with emotion and expressive gestures. Flashes of light dash across the surface against a dark, muted palette of earthy tones suggesting an otherworldly presence. The composition invites the viewer to enter the space and experience the service. Though he used characteristic elements of Baroque composition and was strongly influenced by Venetian painting, Magnasco's loose brushwork, elongated figures, and mysterious subject matter set him apart. Magnasco peers into a world of which he was not part: he was not Jewish and probably perceived Jews as outsiders. At the dawn of the Enlightenment in Europe progressive aristocratic families commissioned paintings by Magnasco, suggesting the painter's support for Enlightenment ideals which included religious tolerance, but Magnasco's personal views on Judaism in Italy remain unknown.

cma:145450.texto: Although this spacious church interior is largely imaginary, Emanuel de Witte’s precise description of architectural forms convinces us that he depicted an actual place. To create a sense of familiarity, he included some specific architectural features from the Oude Kerk (Old Church) in Amsterdam. In the late 1500s, militant Protestant sects occupied Catholic churches in the Netherlands and stripped them of rich decorations and “idolatrous” images. The resulting spare, whitewashed interiors became a favorite subject of Dutch artists, who were intrigued by the interplay of light and shadow over the unadorned walls, and by the challenge of depicting perspectival space.

afirmaciones.texto: La obra representa el interior de una iglesia protestante holandesa con una paleta que incluye tonos cálidos y neutros, dominada por la luz y sombra natural.
La pintura utiliza principalmente tonos cálidos y neutros, no predominan los tonos fríos.
La obra muestra un interior de iglesia con una atmósfera clara y blanca, resultado de la eliminación de decoraciones y el encalado de las paredes, lo que genera un espacio luminoso y despejado.
El uso de blancos y la luz que baña el interior puede interpretarse como una paleta con predominancia de tonos fríos, en contraste con interiores más cálidos.

La paleta de colores parece incluir tonos cálidos y neutros propios del neoclasicismo, sin predominancia clara de tonos fríos.

explicacion.abstencion: No corresponde a la misma iglesia ni presenta tonos fríos.

afirmaciones.texto: La obra representa el interior de una sinagoga con una paleta oscura y terrosa, con tonos apagados y un ambiente místico.
Los tonos predominantes son oscuros y terrosos, no fríos, y la atmósfera es más bien sombría y expresiva.

plan.nota_de_pl3: Las **tres** cláusulas van escritas porque son **tres cosas**: que las dos consultas existan, que difieran del pedido crudo (*rewriting*) y que difieran entre sí (lo que distingue *expansion* de *rewriting*). El veredicto viaja adentro para que las tres cláusulas de las consultas del plan se pueda contar **también sobre una ad-hoc**, cuyo pedido el registro de decisiones no deja guardar.

formato.nota: El formato concreto **sigue abierto**: esto es la **cosmética declarada**, no el contrato. El contrato —`[n]` que asigna el renderizador, toda afirmación con dato citando un `fragment_id` recuperado en esta consulta, 100 % de los CC-BY con atribución, español + cita textual en inglés— vive en el código y es el conteo de referencias colgadas, el criterio de atribución, el criterio de idioma y las obligaciones de la cita.

salida.nota_de_idioma: el contrato de la salida citada / el criterio de idioma: la explicación en **español**, el fragmento citado **textual en inglés, sin traducir**.    El uso de blancos y la luz que baña el interior puede interpretarse como una paleta con predominancia de tonos fríos, en contraste con interiores más cálidos.

   **Fuentes**
   [1] “Although this spacious church interior is largely imaginary, Emanuel de Witte’s precise description of architectural forms convinces us that he depicted an actual place. To create a sense of familiarity, he included some specific architectural features from the Oude Kerk (Old Church) in Amsterdam. In the late 1500s, militant Protestant sects occupied Catholic churches in the Netherlands and stripped them of rich decorations and “idolatrous” images. The resulting spare, whitewashed interiors became a favorite subject of Dutch artists, who were intrigued by the interplay of light and shadow over the unadorned walls, and by the challenge of depicting perspectival space.”
       https://clevelandart.org/art/1971.1 · CC0 1.0

3. **The Obelisk**
   Hubert Robert · 1787 · Oil on canvas · Neoclassicism
   Ficha oficial: https://www.artic.edu/artworks/57049

   La pintura representa un espacio arquitectónico imaginario con vocabulario clásico, con un obelisco y una figura femenina en una hornacina central. [1]
   La paleta de colores parece incluir tonos cálidos y neutros propios del neoclasicismo, sin predominancia clara de tonos fríos.
   No hay indicios en los fragmentos que esta obra represente el mismo interior que la imagen ni que use tonos fríos.

   **Fuentes**
   [1] “This painting is one of four depictions of architectural fantasies by Hubert Robert commissioned by the Marquis de Laborde for his elegant country estate at Méréville, south of Paris. It features a grandiose vaulted space that frames an obelisk, with a peristyle, or colonnade, closing off the distance. Through years of study in Italy, Robert absorbed the vocabulary of Classical architecture and sculpture into his own imaginative language. Here, the female ﬁgure in the central niche is based on a ﬁrst-century sculpture that the artist would have seen during his stay in Rome.”
       https://www.artic.edu/artworks/57049 · CC BY 4.0
       “The Obelisk”, Hubert Robert. Art Institute of Chicago. Texto bajo CC BY 4.0 — https://www.artic.edu/artworks/57049

4. **Interior of a Synagogue**
   Alessandro Magnasco · c. 1725–35 · oil on canvas
   Ficha oficial: https://clevelandart.org/art/1930.22

   La obra representa el interior de una sinagoga con una paleta oscura y terrosa, con tonos apagados y un ambiente místico. [1]
   Los tonos predominantes son oscuros y terrosos, no fríos, y la atmósfera es más bien sombría y expresiva.
   No corresponde a la misma iglesia ni presenta tonos fríos.

   **Fuentes**
   [1] “The Jewish synagogue was among Magnasco's most frequently painted subjects, here presented in a mystical and imaginative way. Expansive architectural space creates room for a multitude of tiny, fantastical figures with elongated limbs. These characters respond to the service with emotion and expressive gestures. Flashes of light dash across the surface against a dark, muted palette of earthy tones suggesting an otherworldly presence. The composition invites the viewer to enter the space and experience the service. Though he used characteristic elements of Baroque composition and was strongly influenced by Venetian painting, Magnasco's loose brushwork, elongated figures, and mysterious subject matter set him apart. Magnasco peers into a world of which he was not part: he was not Jewish and probably perceived Jews as outsiders. At the dawn of the Enlightenment in Europe progressive aristocratic families commissioned paintings by Magnasco, suggesting the painter's support for Enlightenment ideals which included religious tolerance, but Magnasco's personal views on Judaism in Italy remain unknown.”
       https://clevelandart.org/art/1930.22 · CC0 1.0

5. **The Fountains**
   Hubert Robert · 1787–88 · Oil on canvas · Neoclassicism
   Ficha oficial: https://www.artic.edu/artworks/57051

   La obra muestra ruinas clásicas con una paleta que incluye tonos cálidos y neutros, típica del neoclasicismo. [1]
   No hay predominancia de tonos fríos en esta obra, ni representa el mismo interior que la imagen proporcionada.
   No hay evidencia de que esta obra represente el mismo interior en tonos fríos.

   **Fuentes**
   [1] “The painting of Classical ruins had reached the zenith of its popularity when Hubert Robert, the leading French practitioner of this specialty, was commissioned in 1787 to paint a suite of four canvases for a wealthy financier’s château at Méréville, near Paris. The Fountains and its companion pieces were set into the paneled walls of a salon in the château, creating an alternate space that played off of the elegant, Neoclassical decor of the room. Robert has studied in Rome from 1754 to 1765 and there had gleaned his artistic vocabulary. Like the other three large paintings from the group painted for Méréville, all in the Art Institute, The Fountains exploits Robert’s typical vocabulary of fictive niches, arches, coffered vaults, colonnades, majestic stairwells, and Roman statuary to create a fantasy of expansive space. The four paintings are inhabited by tiny figures in the foreground; these serve only to set the scale and animate the scene, for the ruins themselves are the true subject of the pictures. In his use of ruins, Robert embodied the notion of the relationship of mankind and the built environment to nature that was expressed by the French philosopher and encyclopedist Denis Diderot: “Everything vanishes, everything dies, only time endures.””
       https://www.artic.edu/artworks/57051 · CC BY 4.0
       “The Fountains”, Hubert Robert. Art Institute of Chicago. Texto bajo CC BY 4.0 — https://www.artic.edu/artworks/57051
